summary: An April 1 humorous document explaining the origins of the words foo, bar, and foobar, which appear as placeholder names in about 212 RFCs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st RFC investigates why programmers use placeholder names such as foo and bar. It collects possible explanations and examples while treating the subject with comic seriousness.

questions: what does foo mean in programming examples
where did foo and bar come from
subtitle: An April 1st account of the origins and uses of foo, bar, and foobar.

tldr.problem: The RFC observes that many earlier RFCs use foo, bar, and foobar as placeholder names without explaining them.
tldr.mechanism: It defines these metasyntactic variables and surveys possible origins in comic strips, military slang, and computer culture.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3092 is an April 1st informational document. It combines reference-style detail with humorous and sometimes uncertain etymologies.

today: RFC 3092 is listed as Informational and has no obsoleting or updating RFC in the unit metadata. It is an April 1st discussion of technical placeholder words.

sections.title: What Foo and Bar Mean in Examples
sections.content:
The RFC says that about 212 RFCs had used foo, bar, or foobar as metasyntactic variables without defining them. It presents its purpose as explaining the terms for readers, including people for whom English is not a first language.

In this usage, foo is a general sample name, bar commonly follows foo, and foobar combines the two. The RFC also lists other placeholder names used in examples.
sections.plainLanguage: Foo and bar are sample names that stand in for values in examples. This RFC explains the terms and collects possible stories about their origins.

sections.title: Possible Origins of Foo
sections.content:
The RFC traces documented uses of foo through comic strips, including Bill Holman's Smokey Stover, military slang, and other popular culture. It notes appearances in World War II references to foo fighters and describes several competing explanations.

The text uses qualifiers such as probably and cites personal communications, dictionaries, and other sources. It does not present one definitive origin for the word.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC offers several possible paths by which foo entered common use. It does not claim to know one certain origin.

sections.title: Foobar and the RFC Survey
sections.content:
The memo describes foobar as a widely used metasyntactic variable and discusses possible links to military slang and electronics terminology. It also lists acronym expansions for bar, foo, foobar, and FUBAR as examples of how the strings may be interpreted.

An appendix tabulates RFCs in which the terms appear as placeholder variables. The authors distinguish those uses from ordinary occurrences such as the word bar in another context.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix shows how often the placeholder words appeared in RFC examples. The acronym section adds more wordplay rather than one official expansion.
